{{Short description|Abelian group related to division algebras}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Brauer group''' of a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>K</math> is an [[abelian group]] whose elements are [[Morita equivalence]] [[equivalence class|classes]] of [[central simple algebra]]s over <math>K</math>, with addition given by the [[tensor product of algebras]]. It was defined by the algebraist [[Richard Brauer]].

The Brauer group arose out of attempts to classify [[division algebra]]s over a field. It can also be defined in terms of [[Galois cohomology]].  More generally, the Brauer group of a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] is defined in terms of [[Azumaya algebra]]s, or equivalently using [[projective bundle]]s.

== Construction ==
A [[central simple algebra]] (CSA) over a field <math>K</math> is a [[dimension (vector space)|finite-dimensional]] [[associative algebra|associative]] <math>K</math>-[[algebra over a field|algebra]] <math>A</math> such that <math>A</math> is a [[simple ring]] and the [[center (ring theory)|center]] of <math>A</math> is equal to <math>K</math>. Note that CSAs are in general ''not'' division algebras, though CSAs can be used to classify division algebras.

For example, the [[complex number]]s <math>\C</math> form a CSA over themselves, but not over <math>\R</math> (the center is <math>\C</math> itself, hence too large to be CSA over <math>\R</math>). The finite-dimensional division algebras with center <math>\R</math> (that means the dimension over <math>\R</math> is finite) are the [[real number]]s and the [[quaternion]]s by [[Frobenius theorem (real division algebras)|a theorem of Frobenius]], while any [[matrix ring]] over the reals or quaternions – <math>M(n,\R)</math> or <math>M(n,\mathbb{H})</math> – is a CSA over the reals, but not a division algebra (if <math>n>1</math>).

We obtain an [[equivalence relation]] on CSAs over <math>K</math> by the [[Artin–Wedderburn theorem]] ([[Joseph Wedderburn|Wedderburn]]'s part, in fact), to express any CSA as a [[matrix ring]] <math>M(n,D)</math> for some division algebra <math>D</math>. If we look just at <math>D</math>, that is, if we impose an equivalence relation identifying <math>M(m,D)</math> with <math>M(n,D)</math> for all positive [[integer]]s <math>m</math> and <math>n</math>, we get the '''Brauer equivalence''' relation on CSAs over <math>K</math>. The elements of the Brauer group are the Brauer equivalence classes of CSAs over <math>K</math>.

Given central simple algebras <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>, one can look at their [[tensor product of algebras|tensor product]] <math>A\otimes B</math> as a <math>K</math>-algebra. It turns out that this is always central simple. A slick way to see this is to use a characterization: a central simple algebra <math>A</math> over <math>K</math> is a <math>K</math>-algebra that becomes a matrix ring when we extend the field of scalars to an [[algebraic closure]] of <math>K</math>. This result also shows that the dimension of a central simple algebra <math>A</math> as a <math>K</math>-vector space is always a [[square number]]. The '''degree''' of <math>A</math> is defined to be the [[square root]] of its dimension.

As a result, the [[isomorphism class]]es of CSAs over <math>K</math> form a [[monoid]] under tensor product, compatible with Brauer equivalence, and the Brauer classes are all [[invertible]]: the inverse of an algebra <math>A</math> is given by its opposite algebra <math>A^{\mathrm{op}}</math> (the [[opposite ring]] with the same action by <math>K</math> since the image of <math>K\to A</math> is in the center of <math>A</math>). Explicitly, for a CSA <math>A</math> we have <math>A\otimes A^{\mathrm{op}}=M(n^2,K)</math>, where <math>n</math> is the degree of <math>A</math> over <math>K</math>.

The Brauer group of any field is a [[torsion group]]. In more detail, define the '''period''' of a central simple algebra <math>A</math> over <math>K</math> to be its [[order (group theory)|order]] as an element of the Brauer group. Define the '''index''' of <math>A</math> to be the degree of the division algebra that is Brauer equivalent to <math>A</math>. Then the period of <math>A</math> divides the index of <math>A</math> (and hence is finite).{{sfn|Farb|Dennis|1993|loc=Proposition 4.16|ps=none}}

== Examples ==
In the following cases, every finite-dimensional central division algebra over a field <math>K</math> is <math>K</math> itself, so that the Brauer group <math>\operatorname{Br} K</math> is [[trivial group|trivial]]:
* <math>K</math> is an [[algebraically closed field]].
* <math>K</math> is a [[finite field]] ([[Wedderburn's little theorem|Wedderburn's theorem]]).{{sfn|Serre|1979|p=162|ps=none}} Equivalently, every finite [[division ring]] is [[commutative ring|commutative]].
* <math>K</math> is the [[function field of an algebraic variety|function field]] of an [[algebraic curve]] over an algebraically closed field ([[Tsen's theorem]]).{{sfn|Gille|Szamuely|2006|loc=Theorem 6.2.8|ps=none}} More generally, the Brauer group vanishes for any [[quasi-algebraically closed field]].
* <math>K</math> is an [[algebraic extension]] of <math>\Q</math> containing all [[roots of unity]].{{sfn|Serre|1979|p=162|ps=none}}

The Brauer group <math>\operatorname{Br}\R</math> of the real numbers is the [[cyclic group]] of [[order of a group|order]] two. There are just two non-[[isomorphic]] real division algebras with center <math>\R</math>: <math>\R</math> itself and the quaternion algebra <math>\mathbb{H}</math>.{{sfn|Serre|1979|p=163|ps=none}}  Since 
<math>\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{H}\cong M(4,\R)</math>, the class of <math>\mathbb{H}</math> has order two in the Brauer group.

Let <math>K</math> be a [[archimedean property#Definition for normed fields|non-Archimedean]] [[local field]], meaning that <math>K</math> is complete under a [[discrete valuation]] with finite residue field. Then <math>\operatorname{Br}K</math> is isomorphic to <math>\Q/\Z</math>.{{sfn|Serre|1979|p=193|ps=none}}

== Severi–Brauer varieties ==
Another important interpretation of the Brauer group of a field <math>K</math> is that it classifies the [[projective variety|projective varieties]] over <math>K</math> that become isomorphic to [[projective space]] over an algebraic closure of <math>K</math>. Such a variety is called a [[Severi–Brauer variety]], and there is a [[one-to-one correspondence]] between the isomorphism classes of Severi–Brauer varieties of dimension <math>n-1</math> over <math>K</math> and the central simple algebras of degree <math>n</math> over <math>K</math>.{{sfn|Gille|Szamuely|2006|loc=§ 5.2|ps=none}}

For example, the Severi–Brauer varieties of dimension 1 are exactly the [[smooth scheme|smooth]] [[conic]]s in the projective plane over <math>K</math>. For a field <math>K</math> of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] not 2, every conic over <math>K</math> is isomorphic to one of the form <math>ax^2+by^2=z^2</math> for some nonzero elements <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> of <math>K</math>. The corresponding central simple algebra is the [[quaternion algebra]]{{sfn|Gille|Szamuely|2006|loc=Theorem 1.4.2}}
<math display=block>(a,b) = K\langle i,j\rangle/(i^2=a, j^2=b, ij=-ji).</math>
The conic is isomorphic to the projective line <math>\mathbb{P}^1(K)</math> [[if and only if]] the corresponding quaternion algebra is isomorphic to the matrix algebra <math>M(2,K)</math>.

== Cyclic algebras ==
For a positive integer <math>n</math>, let <math>K</math> be a field in which <math>n</math> is invertible such that <math>K</math> contains a [[primitive root of unity|primitive]] <math>n</math>th root of unity <math>\zeta</math>. For nonzero elements <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> of <math>K</math>, the associated '''cyclic algebra''' is the central simple algebra of degree <math>n</math> over <math>K</math> defined by 
<math display=block>(a,b)_{\zeta} = K\langle u,v\rangle/(u^n=a, v^n=b, uv=\zeta vu).</math>
Cyclic algebras are the best-understood central simple algebras. (When <math>n</math> is not invertible in <math>K</math> or <math>K</math> does not have a primitive <math>n</math>th root of unity, a similar construction gives the cyclic algebra <math>(\chi,a)</math> associated to a cyclic <math>\Z/n</math>-extension <math>\chi</math> of <math>K</math> and a nonzero element <math>a</math> of <math>K</math>.{{sfn|Gille|Szamuely|2006|loc=Proposition 2.5.2|ps=none}})

The [[Norm residue isomorphism theorem#History|Merkurjev–Suslin theorem]] in [[algebraic K-theory]] has a strong consequence about the Brauer group. Namely, for a positive integer <math>n</math>, let <math>K</math> be a field in which <math>n</math> is invertible such that <math>K</math> contains a primitive <math>n</math>th root of unity. Then the [[subgroup]] of the Brauer group of <math>K</math> killed by <math>n</math>  is generated by cyclic algebras of degree <math>n</math>.{{sfn|Gille|Szamuely|2006|loc=Theorem 2.5.7|ps=none}} Equivalently, any division algebra of period dividing <math>n</math> is Brauer equivalent to a tensor product of cyclic algebras of degree <math>n</math>. Even for a [[prime number]] <math>p</math>, there are examples showing that a division algebra of period <math>p</math> need not be actually isomorphic to a tensor product of cyclic algebras of degree <math>p</math>.{{sfn|Gille|Szamuely|2006|loc=Remark 2.5.8|ps=none}}

It is a major [[open problem]] (raised by [[Abraham Adrian Albert|Albert]]) whether every division algebra of prime degree over a field is cyclic. This is true if the degree is 2 or 3, but the problem is wide open for primes at least 5. The known results are only for special classes of fields. For example, if <math>K</math> is a [[global field]] or [[local field]], then a division algebra of any degree over <math>K</math> is cyclic, by Albert–[[Richard Brauer|Brauer]]–[[Helmut Hasse|Hasse]]–[[Emmy Noether|Noether]].{{sfn|Pierce|1982|loc=§ 18.6|ps=none}} A "higher-dimensional" result in the same direction was [[mathematical proof|proved]] by Saltman: if <math>K</math> is a field of [[transcendence degree]] 1 over the local field <math>\Q_p</math>, then every division algebra of prime degree <math>\ell\ne p</math> over <math>K</math> is cyclic.{{Sfn|Saltman|2007|ps=none}}

== The period-index problem ==
For any central simple algebra <math>A</math> over a field <math>K</math>, the period of <math>A</math> divides the index of <math>A</math>, and the two numbers have the same prime factors.{{sfn|Gille|Szamuely|2006|loc=Proposition&nbsp;4.5.13|ps=none}} The '''period-index problem''' is to bound the index in terms of the period, for fields <math>K</math> of interest. For example, if <math>A</math> is a central simple algebra over a local field or global field, then Albert–Brauer–Hasse–Noether showed that the index of <math>A</math> is equal to the period of <math>A</math>.{{sfn|Pierce|1982|loc=§ 18.6|ps=none}}

For a central simple algebra <math>A</math> over a field <math>K</math> of transcendence degree <math>n</math> over an algebraically closed field, it is [[conjecture]]d that <math>\operatorname{ind}(A)</math> divides <math>\operatorname{per}(A)^{n-1}</math>. This is true for <math>n\le 2</math>, the case <math>n=2</math> being an important advance by [[Aise Johan de Jong|de Jong]], sharpened in positive characteristic by de&nbsp;Jong–Starr and Lieblich.{{sfn|de Jong|2004|ps=none}}

== Class field theory ==
The Brauer group plays an important role in the modern formulation of [[class field theory]]. If <math>K_v</math> is a non-Archimedean local field, [[local class field theory]] gives a canonical isomorphism <math>\operatorname{inv}_v:\operatorname{Br}K_v\to\Q/\Z</math>, the [[Hasse invariant of an algebra|Hasse invariant]].{{sfn|Serre|1979|p=162|ps=none}}

The case of a global field <math>K</math> (such as a [[number field]]) is addressed by [[global class field theory]]. If <math>D</math> is a central simple algebra over <math>K</math> and <math>v</math> is a [[place (mathematics)|place]] of <math>K</math>, then <math>D\otimes K_v</math> is a central simple algebra over <math>K_v</math>, the completion of <math>K</math> at <math>v</math>. This defines a [[homomorphism]] from the Brauer group of <math>K</math> into the Brauer group of <math>K_v</math>. A given central simple algebra <math>D</math> splits for all but finitely many <math>v</math>, so that the image of <math>D</math> under almost all such homomorphisms is 0. The Brauer group <math>\operatorname{Br}K</math> fits into an [[exact sequence]] constructed by Hasse:{{sfn|Gille|Szamuely|2006|p=159|ps=none}}{{sfn|Pierce|1982|loc=§ 18.5|ps=none}}
<math display=block>0 \rightarrow \operatorname{Br}K \rightarrow \bigoplus_{v \in S} \operatorname{Br}K_v \rightarrow \Q/\Z \rightarrow 0,</math>
where <math>S</math> is the set of all places of <math>K</math> and the right arrow is the sum of the local invariants; the Brauer group of the real numbers is identified with <math>\Z/2\Z</math>. The [[injective|injectivity]] of the left arrow is the content of the [[Albert–Brauer–Hasse–Noether theorem]].

The fact that the sum of all local invariants of a central simple algebra over <math>K</math> is zero is a typical [[reciprocity law#Hilbert reciprocity|reciprocity law]]. For example, applying this to a quaternion algebra <math>(a,b)</math> over <math>\Q</math> gives the [[quadratic reciprocity law]].

== Galois cohomology ==
For an arbitrary field <math>K</math>, the Brauer group can be expressed in terms of [[Galois cohomology]] as follows:{{sfn|Serre|1979|pp=157–159|ps=none}}
<math display=block>\operatorname{Br}K \cong H^2(K, G_\text{m}),</math>
where <math>G_m</math> denotes the [[multiplicative group]], viewed as an [[algebraic group]] over <math>K</math>. More concretely, the cohomology group indicated means <math>H^2(\operatorname{Gal}(K_s/K),K_s^*)</math>, where <math>K_s</math> denotes a [[separable closure]] of ''K''.

The isomorphism of the Brauer group with a Galois cohomology group can be described as follows. The [[automorphism group]] of the algebra of <math>n\times n</math> [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] is the [[projective linear group]] <math>\operatorname{PGL}(n)</math>. Since all central simple algebras over <math>K</math> become isomorphic to the matrix algebra over a separable closure of <math>K</math>, the set of isomorphism classes of central simple algebras of degree <math>n</math> over <math>K</math> can be identified with the Galois cohomology set <math>H^1(K,\operatorname{PGL}(K))</math>. The class of a central simple algebra in <math>H^2(K,G_m)</math> is the image of its class in <math>H^1</math> under the boundary homomorphism
<math display=block>H^1(K, \operatorname{PGL}(n)) \rightarrow H^2(K, G_\text{m})</math>
associated to the [[short exact sequence]] <math>1\to G_m\to\operatorname{GL}(n)\to\operatorname{PGL}(n)\to 1</math>.

== The Brauer group of a scheme ==
The Brauer group was generalized from fields to [[commutative ring]]s by [[Maurice Auslander|Auslander]] and [[Oscar Goldman (mathematician)|Goldman]]. [[Alexander Grothendieck|Grothendieck]] went further by defining the Brauer group of any [[scheme (algebraic geometry)|scheme]].

There are two ways of defining the Brauer group of a scheme <math>X</math>, using either [[Azumaya algebra]]s over <math>X</math> or [[projective bundle]]s over <math>X</math>. The second definition involves projective bundles that are locally trivial in the [[étale topology]], not necessarily in the [[Zariski topology]]. In particular, a projective bundle is defined to be zero in the Brauer group if and only if it is the projectivization of some vector bundle.

The '''cohomological Brauer group''' of a [[quasi-compact morphism|quasi-compact]] scheme <math>X</math> is defined to be the [[torsion subgroup]] of the [[étale cohomology]] group <math>H^2(X,G_m)</math>. (The whole group <math>H^2(X,G_m)</math> need not be torsion, although it is torsion for [[regular, integral, quasi-compact scheme]]s <math>X</math>.{{sfn|Milne|1980|loc=p.107|ps=none}}) The Brauer group is always a subgroup of the cohomological Brauer group. [[Ofer Gabber|Gabber]] showed that the Brauer group is equal to the cohomological Brauer group for any scheme with an [[ample line bundle]] (for example, any [[quasi-projective variety|quasi-projective]] scheme over a commutative ring).{{sfn|de Jong|loc=A result of Gabber|ps=none}}

The whole group <math>H^2(X,G_m)</math> can be viewed as classifying the [[gerbe]]s over <math>X</math> with structure group <math>G_m</math>.

For smooth projective varieties over a field, the Brauer group is an important [[birational geometry|birational]] invariant. For example, when <math>X</math> is also [[rationally connected variety|rationally connected]] over the complex numbers, the Brauer group of <math>X</math> is isomorphic to the torsion subgroup of the [[singular cohomology]] group <math>H^3(X,\Z)</math>, which is therefore a birational invariant. [[Michael Artin|Artin]] and [[David Mumford|Mumford]] used this description of the Brauer group to give the first example of a [[unirational variety]] <math>X</math> over <math>\C</math> that is not stably rational (that is, no product of <math>X</math> with a projective space is rational).{{sfn|Colliot-Thélène|1995|loc=Proposition 4.2.3 and § 4.2.4|ps=none}}

== Relation to the Tate conjecture ==
Artin conjectured that every [[proper scheme]] over the integers has finite Brauer group.{{sfn|Milne|1980|loc=Question IV.2.19|ps=none}} This is far from known even in the special case of a smooth projective variety <math>X</math> over a finite field. Indeed, the finiteness of the Brauer group for surfaces in that case is equivalent to the [[Tate conjecture]] for [[divisor (algebraic geometry)|divisor]]s on <math>X</math>, one of the main problems in the theory of [[algebraic cycle]]s.{{sfn|Tate|1994|loc=Proposition 4.3|ps=none}}

For a regular [[glossary of algebraic geometry#integral|integral]] scheme of dimension 2 which is [[flat morphism|flat]] and proper over the [[ring of integers]] of a number field, and which has a [[section (fiber bundle)|section]], the finiteness of the Brauer group is equivalent to the finiteness of the [[Tate–Shafarevich group]] {{math|Ш}} for the [[Jacobian variety]] of the general fiber (a curve over a number field).{{sfn|Grothendieck|1968|loc=Le groupe de Brauer III, Proposition&nbsp;4.5|ps=none}} The finiteness of {{math|Ш}} is a central problem in the arithmetic of [[elliptic curve]]s and more generally [[abelian variety|abelian varieties]].

== The Brauer–Manin obstruction ==
Let <math>X</math> be a smooth projective variety over a number field <math>K</math>. The [[Hasse principle]] would predict that if <math>X</math> has a [[rational point]] over all completions <math>K_v</math> of <math>K</math>, then <math>X</math> has a <math>K</math>-rational point. The Hasse principle holds for some special classes of varieties, but not in general. [[Yuri Manin|Manin]] used the Brauer group of <math>X</math> to define the [[Brauer–Manin obstruction]], which can be applied in many cases to show that <math>X</math> has no <math>K</math>-points even when <math>X</math> has points over all completions of <math>K</math>.
